newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila-Beijing row mounts over rocks.
newsitem.headline: Manila-Beijing row mounts over rocks.

text.p: A row between the Philippines and China over barely visible rocks in the South China Sea escalated on Tuesday when Beijing protested against the arrest of 21 Chinese fishermen in the disputed area.

Chinese Consul-General Shi Bingyi demanded the release of the fishermen, saying they were in Chinese territory when a Philippine Navy ship apprehended the vessel and its crew last week off Scarborough Shoal, which both countries claim.

The latest diplomatic clash between the two countries broke out while Filipino and Chinese senior officials were meeting in Beijing to try to defuse growing tension over their rival claims to tiny islands and rocky outcrops in the South China Sea.
"The Chinese fishermen have every right to fish in Huang Yan island (Scarborough Shoal) because it's part of Chinese territory," a Filipino diplomat quoted Shi as saying.
Beijing insists all the islands, reefs and rocks in the South China Sea historically belong to China and cites 700-year-old documents to back its claim.
Manila says the 16-km (10-mile) rock formation lies within its exclusive economic zone, giving it ownership.
The rocks, which almost disappear at high tide and are little more than a resting place for smugglers, lie 200 km (125 miles) west of the Philippines' mainland Zambales province.
It was the third time this month that the two countries have tangled over the rocks.

China earlier protested against the hoisting by Filipinos of their national flag over the rocks. It protested again when a group of Philippine congressmen sailed to the shoal to be photographed standing under the flag.
A navy spokesman said the Chinese fishermen and their vessel were apprehended on May 20.

Two days after their arrest -- which Manila kept secret -- President Fidel Ramos adopted a conciliatory tone, telling financiers in Hong Kong that Manila was ready to settle disputes with China by peaceful negotiations.
News of the fishermen's detention was unknown until Shi strode into the Foreign Ministry on Tuesday and demanded their release.
"It is in everyone's interest to lower the alarm levels and temperature level," Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Ciazon told reporters after China's protest.
The shoal lies well north of the Spratly Islands, a cluster of potentially oil-rich isles, reefs and atolls that the two countries are also squabbling over.
The Spratlys are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, Malaysia and Brunei.
